title_en: Shanghai Animation Film Studio v. Electronic Industry Press and Qu Jianfang — dispute over copyright ownership and infringement
ruling_gist_en: The ownership of copyright in works made for hire in a specific historical period should not be determined directly by applying the criteria for ownership of works made for hire under the current Copyright Law. In this case, Shanghai Animation Film Studio (hereinafter referred to as SAFS) and Qu Jianfang filed a lawsuit to assert ownership of the copyright in the character design works in question more than thirty years after the creation of the works. During this period, the coexistence of the use of the works by SAFS and Qu Jianfang was an objective fact, and both parties have contributed to the enhancement of the social influence and brand value of the character designs in question. Under these circumstances, if the property rights in the copyright of the works in question were to be exclusively owned by one party, it would obviously lead to an imbalance of rights and would also violate the principle of fairness.

full_text_en:
Shanghai Animation Film Studio v. Publishing House of Electronics Industry and Qu Jianfang — dispute over copyright ownership and infringement

【Ruling Summary】

The determination of copyright ownership for works created in the course of employment during a specific historical period should not directly apply the criteria established under the current Copyright Law for judging the ownership of rights in such works. In this case, Shanghai Animation Film Studio (hereinafter referred to as "SAFS") and Qu Jianfang brought litigation to assert copyright ownership over the character design works in question more than thirty years after the creation of the works. During this period, a de facto coexistence existed whereby both SAFS and Qu Jianfang separately used the works in question. Moreover, both parties contributed to enhancing the social influence and brand value of the character designs in question. Under such circumstances, vesting the economic rights in the copyright of the works in question solely in one party would clearly result in an imbalance of rights and would also violate the principle of fairness.

Plaintiff (Counterclaim Defendant): Shanghai Animation Film Studio, domiciled at Wanhangdu Road, Jing'an District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Qian Jianping, Factory Director.

Defendant (Counterclaim Plaintiff): Qu Jianfang, male, 80 years old, domiciled in Xuhui District, Shanghai.

Defendant: Publishing House of Electronics Industry, domiciled at Wanshou Road, Haidian District, Beijing.
Legal Representative: Ao Ran, President.

The plaintiff, Shanghai Animation Film Studio (hereinafter referred to as "SAFS"), filed a lawsuit with the Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai against the defendants Qu Jianfang and the Publishing House of Electronics Industry (hereinafter referred to as "the Publishing House") regarding a dispute over copyright ownership and infringement.

Plaintiff SAFS alleged: The plaintiff is the copyright owner of the puppet animation series *The Story of Afanti*, which was filmed between 1979 and 1989 and adapted from the folk tales of *The Story of Afanti* circulating among the Xinjiang people. The series won the Best Animation Film Award at the Third China Film "Hundred Flowers Awards" in 1980 and the first prize for animation films in the 1994 National Ethnic Minority Theme Film "Soaring Dragon Awards". The plaintiff purchased two books entitled *The Classic Comics of Afanti* and *The Selected Stories of Afanti* published by the defendant Publishing House and illustrated by the defendant Qu Jianfang. The covers and contents of the said books featured the images of Afanti, Mr. Bayi, and the Little Donkey from the puppet animation series *The Story of Afanti*. The plaintiff contended that copyright in the character images of Afanti, Mr. Bayi, and the Little Donkey, in both three-dimensional puppet form and static two-dimensional drawings, belongs to the plaintiff. The defendants, without permission, used the characters from the puppet animation *The Story of Afanti*, to which the plaintiff owns the copyright, for profit, thereby infringing upon the plaintiff's lawful rights and interests. The plaintiff requested the court to order: 1. The two defendants to cease infringement and stop selling and using the infringing products; 2. The two defendants to pay the plaintiff compensation in the amount of RMB 200,000 (hereinafter all amounts are in RMB unless otherwise stated).

Defendant Publishing House argued:
1. In 1978, the defendant Qu Jianfang created the three artistic images of Afanti and others. The *Selected Models of Chinese Art Films* published by Shanghai People's Fine Arts Publishing House in 1980 indicated that the author of the Afanti artwork was Qu Jianfang. In 1996, Qu Jianfang obtained a copyright registration certificate for the artistic images in question. For a long time, Qu Jianfang has actively exercised the copyright in the artistic images in question, conducted extensive and artistically profound promotional work for the images, and actively initiated multiple enforcement actions. Relevant people's court judgments have confirmed Qu Jianfang's status as the copyright holder. The artistic images in question constitute "general works created in the course of employment," and the copyright therein is enjoyed by the original creator, Qu Jianfang.
2. Before publishing the books in question, the Publishing House signed a book publishing contract with Qu Jianfang, which contained clauses on warranty against defects in rights. Moreover, based on the aforementioned publicly available publications, copyright registration certificates, court judgments, and media reports, it was sufficient for the public to believe that Qu Jianfang held the copyright in the artistic images in question. As the publisher of the books in question, the Publishing House fulfilled its reasonable duty of care, was not at fault subjectively, and did not constitute infringement.
3. The books in question were published in May 2010, and the plaintiff SAFS's lawsuit has exceeded the statute of limitations. The Publishing House requested the dismissal of the plaintiff's claims.

Defendant Qu Jianfang's defense and counterclaim:
In 1978, while serving as the art designer for the puppet film *Afanti: Sowing Gold*, Qu Jianfang created the two-dimensional character artistic images of Afanti, Mr. Bayi, and the Little Donkey, and is the creator of these artistic images. The three-dimensional puppets made based on these artistic images were merely reproductions of the two-dimensional artworks. On June 20, 1979, before the public release of the puppet film *Afanti: Sowing Gold*, Qu Jianfang first published the artistic images of Afanti and others in the *New Youth* periodical. At that time, the plaintiff SAFS did not implement a remuneration system for creators. To produce excellent animation works and encourage artists to create outstanding character images, SAFS acknowledged that creators could submit works for external publication and receive remuneration. Subsequently, Qu Jianfang continuously submitted the artistic images of Afanti and others for publication, published them in periodicals and magazines under his own name, and served as director and art designer for the filming of the 13-episode puppet animation series *The Story of Afanti*, until his resignation in January 1989. After resigning, Qu Jianfang consistently worked to promote the character images of Afanti and actively asserted and exercised the rights of publication, authorship, reproduction, adaptation, and production of the Afanti artistic images. This included: in 1990, Qu Jianfang filming *The New Story of Afanti: The Disobedient Dog* at Dalian Afanti International Animation Company; between 2004 and 2012, cooperating with the defendant Publishing House to publish numerous series of books featuring the Afanti artistic images; starting from 2004, licensing the Afanti artistic images to numerous enterprises for use and authorizing others to produce three-dimensional animated Afanti images; in 2005 and 2007, actively enforcing rights against infringement, with relevant court civil judgments confirming that the copyright in the Afanti artistic images belonged to Qu Jianfang; around 2010, authorizing Shanghai Afanti Investment Holdings Co., Ltd. to produce a six-episode series *Young and Old Afanti*. Before the enactment of the Copyright Law, the natural rights in the Afanti artistic images were exercised by Qu Jianfang. SAFS only used the Afanti artistic images within the film domain and never independently asserted or exercised the copyright in them. After the Copyright Law was enacted, Qu Jianfang registered the copyright in the Afanti artistic images in 1996 and actively exercised the copyright. SAFS continued to exercise its copyright in the *Afanti* series of art films within the scope of its art film business, and its enforcement activities were limited to the overall copyright of the animated films. Qu Jianfang and SAFS each exercised their rights in accordance with the Copyright Law. SAFS was fully aware that Qu Jianfang had registered the copyright, extensively published series of books featuring the Afanti artistic images, widely licensed the use of the Afanti artistic images to third parties, and that effective civil judgments from relevant courts had confirmed that the copyright in the Afanti artistic images belonged to Qu Jianfang. However, SAFS took no legal action to assert ownership or enforce rights, nor did it independently exercise the copyright in the Afanti artistic images. This demonstrates that SAFS recognized the artistic images in question as works created in the course of employment, with copyright belonging to Qu Jianfang. The right of authorship for a legal person work belongs to the legal person. However, in *Selected Models of Chinese Art Films* edited by SAFS in 1980, the author of the Afanti artwork was clearly indicated as Qu Jianfang. Moreover, the artistic images of characters like Afanti embody a highly individualized act of artistic creation, and the creative process reflects Qu Jianfang's personal will. Therefore, the works in question are not legal person works. The completion and success of the works in question primarily depended on the author's intellectual creative activity and artistic skill. They do not fall under the category of "special works created in the course of employment" that mainly utilize the unit's material and technical conditions. There is no provision in laws or regulations, nor any agreement between Qu Jianfang and SAFS, that vests the copyright in the works in question in SAFS. Hence, there is no circumstance of "special works created in the course of employment" as defined by the Copyright Law. They constitute "general works created in the course of employment," and the copyright is enjoyed by the author, Qu Jianfang. SAFS has the right to preferentially use the works within its business scope. Starting in 1986, SAFS implemented a remuneration system for creators, providing them with payments far exceeding their salaries. However, Qu Jianfang created the Afanti artistic works before this system, and he did not receive any additional rewards, remuneration, or compensation for creating the works in question thereafter. In January 1989, Qu Jianfang was forced to resign from SAFS, leaving the system. He did not benefit from staff housing allocation within the system, nor did he enjoy the medical insurance and other welfare benefits for retired cadres that he might have enjoyed as a first-batch senior-level art designer in 1988. The reason the Afanti character images have become universally recognized and beloved artistic images is attributable to Qu Jianfang's continuous external use or authorization of others to use these character images over the past thirty years. Considering all these factors and from the perspective of fairness, the copyright in the works in question should also be enjoyed by Qu Jianfang. In summary, Qu Jianfang requested the dismissal of the plaintiff SAFS's claims and filed a counterclaim seeking confirmation that he enjoys the copyright in the artistic images of Afanti, Mr. Bayi, and the Little Donkey.

Plaintiff SAFS argued in response:
In 1978, SAFS decided to adapt and produce the *Story of Afanti* series of puppet films based on existing Xinjiang folk tales. The overall creation was led by directors Jin Xi and Liu Huiyi, the script was written by screenwriter Ling Shu, and the art design and character modeling were done by the defendant Qu Jianfang and Sun Daheng. These individuals, together with other creators, formed the production team, made multiple trips to Xinjiang for fieldwork, where Qu Jianfang completed the two-dimensional design for the Afanti animation theme, and Sun Daheng turned this two-dimensional design into puppet models. Ultimately, in 1979, they jointly completed the processing steps of carving, makeup, costume, puppet movement, and background creation, filming the puppet film *Afanti: Sowing Gold*. The formation of the character designs for Afanti, Mr. Bayi, and the Little Donkey occurred after SAFS approved the project, based on the director's overall concept and the determined overall style, the story framework and character building from the script, and the relevant materials collected by the production team during the Xinjiang fieldwork. The main drafting was done by Qu Jianfang, but all creative and production processes and personnel arrangements were decided by SAFS, and all funding was provided by SAFS. The final confirmation and adoption of the designs were also decided by SAFS. The production of the film in question took place before the Copyright Law was enacted, during the planned economy period. As an employee of SAFS engaged in art design, completing the relevant work tasks was part of Qu Jianfang's duties. Only by completing the assigned work tasks could Qu Jianfang receive his salary, bonuses, and welfare benefits such as medical care. The principle that fruits of labor created in fulfilling work tasks belong to the legal person was a universally recognized code of conduct and an industry practice at that time. Therefore, the character designs of Afanti, Mr. Bayi, and the Little Donkey were created jointly by the main creative members of the production team under the auspices and leadership of SAFS. They should be considered legal person works, with the copyright belonging to SAFS. During the filming process, SAFS instructed its creators not to submit works for external publication. Qu Jianfang abided by this rule in practice, indicating that both parties recognized SAFS's right to control the character designs in question. On the principle of good faith, Qu Jianfang should not later express a contrary intention and claim copyright in the character design artworks in question. The fact that SAFS did not intervene in Qu Jianfang's external publication of the designs after the film was completed, or when it did not assert rights in related infringement lawsuits, cannot be interpreted as a statement on ownership. It does not mean SAFS waived its rights, but merely chose not to exercise them, as SAFS's copyright was not challenged during this process. Even if the character designs constitute works created in the course of employment, they fall under the category of "special works created in the course of employment" as provided in Article 16, Paragraph 2, Item (2) of the Copyright Law. Qu Jianfang only enjoys the right of authorship, with all other copyright rights belonging to SAFS. In summary, SAFS requested the dismissal of the counterclaimant Qu Jianfang's counterclaims.

The Xuhui District People's Court of Shanghai found the following facts at first instance:

I. Overview of the defendant Qu Jianfang's employment history at the plaintiff SAFS

In 1957, the defendant Qu Jianfang began working at the plaintiff SAFS, serving successively as art designer, director, and other roles. In March 1988, Qu Jianfang was promoted to the rank of first-level art designer. In December 1988, SAFS made a decision regarding Qu Jianfang's service as Chairman of the Board of Dalian Afanti International Animation Company: 1. Qu Jianfang's appointment to the professional position of first-level art designer was terminated, and the salary corresponding to the position was not to be paid; 2. Qu Jianfang was required to complete resignation procedures before the end of December 1988; failing to do so would result in automatic resignation. On January 26, 1989, Qu Jianfang submitted a resignation letter to SAFS, stating as the reason: "Since November 21, 1988, I have been serving as Chairman of the Board of Afanti International Animation Company. Due to work commitments, I can no longer concurrently hold my position at the factory." In the same month, SAFS issued a certificate of resignation, approving Qu Jianfang's resignation, and Qu Jianfang officially severed his relationship with SAFS effective February 1, 1989.

II. Creation, release, credits, and awards of the "Afanti" puppet film

In 1978, Ling Shu, a screenwriter at the plaintiff SAFS, created the literary script for the art film *Afanti: Sowing Gold* based on Xinjiang folk tales. After SAFS approved it, a production team was formed, with Jin Xi and Liu Huiyi assigned as directors and the defendant Qu Jianfang as art designer. The production team made several trips to Xinjiang for fieldwork to enrich the visual material for the film. Subsequently, Qu Jianfang drew the character designs for Afanti, Bayi, and the Little Donkey, which, after being reviewed and approved by SAFS, were made into puppets for filming. In 1979, SAFS completed the production of the puppet film *Afanti: Sowing Gold* (i.e., the film at issue). At that time, SAFS had no regulations concerning the ownership of rights in works. The main characteristics of the Afanti design were: an elongated head shape, a high forehead, leaf-shaped eyebrows, black bean-like eyes, a curved and highly upturned nose, a small mouth, small ears, curly upturned goatee, a thin neck, a body shape that was thin on top and thick on the bottom, a long upper body, a head wrapped in a white turban, a long white outer robe, and black leather boots with highly upturned toes. The main characteristics of the Bayi design were: a round face, a small round hat on the head, hedgehog-like eyes, a bulbous nose, a large mouth with missing teeth, protruding ears, slanted eyebrows, a mustache, a large belly, and an obese body shape. The main characteristics of the Little Donkey were: large round eyes with much white showing, long ears, the upper half of the face in a dark color and the lower half in a light color, a large head with a small body, a long thin neck, and thin legs.

A film catalog compiled by the Shanghai Film Bureau in 1982 showed that the puppet film *Afanti: Sowing Gold* was released domestically and internationally on September 17, 1979.

From 1981 to 1987, the plaintiff SAFS continued to film thirteen episodes of the puppet film series *The Story of Afanti*, using the character images of Afanti and the Little Donkey from *Sowing Gold*, with the defendant Qu Jianfang serving as director and also as art designer.

During the trial of this case, the plaintiff SAFS stated that after the *Afanti* puppet film was completed, it was first screened in cinemas, then broadcast on television. In the early 1990s, VCDs were produced and distributed, and after 2000, DVDs were produced and distributed. Distribution also included books. The defendant Qu Jianfang stated that he was unaware of SAFS's distribution in the form of CDs and books.

In the December 1980 issue of the *Film Culture* periodical, an article by the defendant Qu Jianfang titled "A Preliminary Exploration of Afanti's Design" was published. In the article, Qu Jianfang stated: "Initially, I used traditional Han decorative transformation techniques, but the image I designed never felt like a Uyghur, lacking Uyghur characteristics. Its form was also inconsistent with Afanti's humorous and sharp style. Later, I sought and borrowed expressive techniques suitable for shaping the Afanti image from Xinjiang murals and unearthed cultural relics... On the basis of absorbing and borrowing from the Uyghur cultural and artistic traditions, we found a correct path to explore a national style." "When designing the model... I paid attention to using humorous deformation and exaggeration to highlight the character's personality." "When designing Afanti's clothing and props, I also started from the perspective of portraying the character... everywhere expressing Afanti's humorous personality." "In the process of making the puppets, the choice of materials for craft processing was also an important means of bringing out and embodying the 'puppet flavor'... We decided to use silk material to make the puppets, to enhance the craftsmanship and aesthetic feeling of the puppets."

In the book *Research on Art Film Creation* published by China Film Press in March 1984, an article by Jin Xi and Liu Huiyi titled "Director's Notes on *Afanti*" was included. In the article, the two directors stated: "The literary script provided the first visual foundation for the film's production. Immersion in life then provided a certain degree of supplement and modification to this visual foundation, thus beginning the design engineering of the film's shooting blueprint." "The comic technique and bold brushstrokes were a necessary explanation for the unification of the film's overall style in terms of modeling, background, character movement, and even scene transitions. With this explanation, the various components of the comprehensive art form had a unified creative direction. For example, although Afanti is a positive character, to unify the overall style and comic technique, the art design colleague abandoned the general notion of not daring to exaggerate positive characters..."

The final shooting script of *Sowing Gold* and the staff list shown at the beginning of *Sowing Gold* in the *Afanti* series DVD released by SAFS and distributed by Shanghai Film and Audio Publishing House were: Adaptation: Ling Shu; Directors: Jin Xi, Liu Huiyi; Art Designer: Qu Jianfang; Model Maker: Sun Daheng; Sets: Cheng Zhongyue, Chen Shaoyuan; Cinematography: Zhu Dingyuan; Animation Design: Lü Heng, Guo Yan, Kong Fanchun, Cai Yuanlan, Jin Fangling, Jin Shangxia, Li Guofen; Composer: Wu Yingju; Sound: Lu Zhongbo; Editing: Mo Puzhong, Lu Baoguo; Special Effects: Lü Jingtang; Producer: Guan Airu; Soloist: Ma Guoguang; Performed by: Orchestra of the Art Department of the Central Institute for Nationalities; Conductor: Jin Zhengping.

The *Selected Models of Chinese Art Films*, compiled by the plaintiff SAFS and published by Shanghai People's Fine Arts Publishing House in October 1980, included the character designs of Afanti, Bayi, and the Little Donkey, credited as "Qu Jianfang".

In the 30th-anniversary commemorative album compiled by the plaintiff SAFS in July 1987, the defendant Qu Jianfang was introduced as follows: "After graduating from the Oil Painting Department of the Lu Xun Academy of Fine Arts in 1957, he joined 'SAFS'. He participated in the set painting for three films, including the animation film... then shifted to puppet films, serving as art designer for over twenty films, including... In 1979, the Afanti image he designed and modeled was most successful. Subsequently, he directed multiple episodes of *Afanti*, winning people's acclaim... Now, he is still continuing to film *Afanti*, with a planned total of thirteen episodes."

III. Copyright Registration, Use, or Authorization of the Involved Artistic Images by Defendant Qu Jianfang

In February 1988, Defendant Qu Jianfang, in the *Advanced Professional and Technical Position Evaluation Report Form* for promotion to First-Class Art Designer, filled out the following under "Main Achievements and Major Works (Papers)": In 1979, he served as the art designer for the puppet film *Avanti: Planting Gold*; from 1981 to 1987, he served as the director and art designer for the 13-episode puppet series *The Story of Avanti*; in 1983, the Xinjiang People's Publishing House published *Planting Gold*, a single-volume color picture book; in 1986, he created the decorative illustrations for the book *The Story of Little Avanti* published by Shanghai Children's Publishing House. Te Wei, the first director of Plaintiff Meiying Film Studio, wrote in the *Peer Expert Evaluation Opinion Form*: "At Meiying Film Studio, Qu Jianfang is one of the most creative art designers, capable of adapting to various themes and artistic styles and creating vivid character images. His representative works include *Avanti*, etc. The *Avanti* character design has been widely praised in the art world."

In 1980, *Avanti: Planting Gold* won the "Best Animated Film Award" at the 3rd Hundred Flowers Awards for Popular Cinema. In April 1980, three animated films produced by Plaintiff Meiying Film Studio, including *Avanti: Planting Gold*, won the Ministry of Culture's 1979 "Outstanding Film Award". In May 1980, the Film Bureau of the Ministry of Culture issued a notice to Meiying Film Studio regarding "Issuance of the 1979 Outstanding Film Award Bonus", stating that the three award-winning films would receive a total bonus of RMB 4,300. In Annex 2, "Measures for the Distribution of the 'Outstanding Film Award' Bonus", it was required that for animated films, 60% of the bonus be distributed to the main creative personnel (including screenwriter, director, art designer, animation designer, background painter, cinematographer, composer, sound engineer, and editor). During the trial of this case, Defendant Qu Jianfang stated that he had not received this bonus, and even if it had been issued, according to the bonus distribution method, each person would have received less than RMB 51, which was insufficient to affect the ownership of the copyright in the involved artistic images.

From January 1, 1986, Plaintiff Meiying Film Studio improved its bonus distribution method and implemented a remuneration system for creative personnel.

IV. Rights Protection Regarding the Involved Artistic Images and Media Coverage

In November 2004, Defendant Qu Jianfang filed a lawsuit on the grounds that others had used the Avanti image in television commercials without authorization, infringing his copyright. In June 2005, the Wuhan Intermediate People's Court of Hubei Province, in Civil Judgment No. (2005) Wu Zhi Chu Zi No. 32, determined that Qu Jianfang was the author of the series of Avanti artistic image works and held the copyright, and ordered the defendant in that case to cease infringement, compensate for losses, and publish a statement in *China Intellectual Property News* apologizing to Qu Jianfang. The beginning of that judgment stated Qu Jianfang's identity as "Chairman of Shanghai Avanti Cartoon Art Co., Ltd."

On August 5, 2006, the Shanghai Channel of Eastday.com published an article titled "'Father of Avanti' Inscribes for Eastday Netizens; New 'Avanti' to Be Filmed Next Year," with pictorial coverage of Defendant Qu Jianfang's book signing event for the *Avanti Series Books* at the 2006 Shanghai Book Fair and his improvised drawing of the Avanti image.

In December 2006, Defendant Qu Jianfang filed a lawsuit on the grounds that others had used the Avanti image on websites for advertising without authorization, infringing his copyright. In June 2007, the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, in Civil Judgment No. (2007) Er Zhong Min Chu Zi No. 210, addressing the defendant's claim that Qu Jianfang did not hold the copyright in the Avanti artistic image, determined that Qu Jianfang held independent copyright in the Avanti artistic image he created, and ordered the defendant to cease infringement, compensate for losses, and publish a statement on its website apologizing to Qu Jianfang. The judgment became final. On August 7, 2007, China Court Net published an article titled "'Avanti' Artistic Image Copyright Protected; Creator Awarded Compensation," reporting the above judgment. Sina Finance Net and Legal Net republished the report. On August 8, 2007, *The Beijing News* published an article titled "'Father of Avanti' Wins First Instance Compensation of RMB 50,000 in Rights Protection," and *Jinghua Times* published an article titled "'Avanti' Image Author Wins Infringement Lawsuit," also reporting the above judgment.

In June 2008, *Hope Monthly*, Issue No. 73, published an exclusive interview with Defendant Qu Jianfang, titled "Interview with the 'Father of Avanti' — Mr. Qu Jianfang, Creator of China's Avanti Image," introducing how Qu Jianfang entered the animation film industry, his process of creating the Avanti artistic image, his personal study and work experience (including serving as Chairman, General Manager, and Artistic Director of Dalian Avanti International Animation Company from 1989, and concurrently as Chairman of Shanghai Avanti Cartoon Art Co., Ltd. from 1998), and his related positions, accompanied by photos of Qu Jianfang and his on-site book signing, and designs of Avanti and his little donkey.

In July 2008, Plaintiff Meiying Film Studio filed a lawsuit on the grounds that others had used the Avanti and donkey images without authorization on the packaging covers and disc surfaces of VCDs of *The Story of Avanti* published, distributed, and sold, infringing its copyright. In December 2008, the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province, in Civil Judgment No. (2008) Hang Min San Chu Zi No. 299, held that *Avanti* (puppet film) was produced by Meiying Film Studio, and in the absence of contrary evidence, confirmed that Meiying Film Studio held the copyright in the puppet images of Avanti and the little donkey, and rendered a default judgment ordering the defendant to cease infringement and compensate for losses.

In March 2008, Plaintiff Meiying Film Studio entered into a licensing agreement with the Business Department of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited, licensing the business department to use the film animation images from *The Story of Avanti* on bank cards. In October 2008, Defendant Qu Jianfang filed a lawsuit with the Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai [Case No. (2008) Pu Min San (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 449] against the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited and China UnionPay Co., Ltd., on the grounds that the UnionPay credit cards issued by them used the Avanti artistic image without permission, infringing his copyright. During the trial of that case, Qu Jianfang indicated that he would not assert rights against Meiying Film Studio. In November 2008, the court notified Meiying Film Studio to participate as a third party. Meiying Film Studio stated in that case that the patterns used on the bank cards were film screenshots it had authorized, which were puppet images, and argued that Qu Jianfang did not hold the copyright in the Avanti image, and that the copyright in the *Avanti* film and its character images belonged to Meiying Film Studio. In January 2009, Qu Jianfang applied to withdraw the lawsuit against China UnionPay Co., Ltd., and the court granted it. In February 2009, because the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited was not the proper defendant (the proper defendant should have been the Business Department of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited), Qu Jianfang agreed, but considering the litigation costs of withdrawal, requested the court to directly dismiss the lawsuit. The court thus rendered a ruling dismissing the lawsuit on the grounds of incorrect defendant.

During the trial of this case, Defendant Qu Jianfang stated that the actual outcome of the above case was that the parties reached a settlement: he sold RMB 50,000 worth of *Avanti* series promotional materials to "Xinjiang Industrial and Commercial Bank," and he authorized the bank to use the Avanti artistic image to produce and issue credit cards, thereby resolving the dispute. He submitted the *Contract for Authorizing Use of 'Avanti' Image and Appointing 'Avanti' Credit Card Image Ambassador* signed in February 2010 with the Business Department of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited (which stipulated that Qu Jianfang would not raise any objections or file any lawsuits regarding the bank's prior use of Avanti artistic images taken from film screenshots provided by Plaintiff Meiying Film Studio for making credit cards), a *Purchase and Sales Contract*, and bank account statements. Meiying Film Studio did not object to the authenticity of the above evidence but stated that it was unclear whether the contracts had been performed. Additionally, Meiying Film Studio stated that although it had not appealed the effective judgments of the Wuhan Intermediate People's Court of Hubei Province and the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, it had raised an objection to the Shanghai Copyright Bureau regarding Qu Jianfang's copyright registration. The Copyright Bureau directed it to resolve the matter through litigation. At the time, considering that Qu Jianfang was a long-time employee, it did not file a lawsuit. It was only when compelled that it initiated the present lawsuit.

On August 15, 2010, the Shanghai Channel of Xinhua Net published an article titled "Meeting Avanti at the Children's Book Carnival," reporting that Defendant Qu Jianfang attended the 2010 Shanghai Book Fair with *Avanti Story Selections* for a book signing event, accompanied by photos of Qu Jianfang signing books and interacting with children.

V. Publication and Distribution of the Allegedly Infringing Books

On February 8, 2010, Defendant Qu Jianfang and Defendant Electronics Publishing House signed *Publishing Contracts* for the publication of two books, *Avanti Story Selections (Beautifully Illustrated Edition)* and *Avanti Classic Comics (Collector's Edition)*. Qu Jianfang granted the Electronics Publishing House the exclusive right to publish and distribute the above books in China (including Mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan) in paper book form. The Electronics Publishing House was to pay Qu Jianfang royalties based on the royalty method [book price × royalty rate (8% and 7%, respectively) × actual number of copies sold]. The contracts were valid for 10 years, and if neither party objected upon expiration, they would automatically extend for another 10 years. Article 5 of the contracts stipulated: "Party A (Qu Jianfang) warrants that it is the copyright owner of this work or the representative of the copyright owner of this work... If the exercise of the above rights infringes the copyright or exclusive publishing right of others, Party A shall bear full responsibility..." Article 7 stipulated: "Party A warrants that this work does not infringe the copyright, exclusive publishing right, or other legitimate rights of others... If Party A uses content from others' works in this work, it shall strictly comply with the relevant provisions of the Chinese Copyright Law and list the names of the used works and the authors in this work..."

In May 2010, Defendant Electronics Publishing House published and distributed *Avanti Story Selections (Beautifully Illustrated Edition)* and *Avanti Classic Comics (Collector's Edition)*. Both books used the involved artistic images. The former book was attributed to "Adapted by Wang Ya, Illustrated by Qu Jianfang," and the latter was attributed to "Compiled by Avanti International Animation Company." The book prices were RMB 14.80 and RMB 29, respectively. The print runs of these two books submitted by Meiying Film Studio were the 7th printing in December 2011 and the 3rd printing in October 2010, respectively. The print runs of these two books submitted by Defendant Qu Jianfang were the 8th printing in March 2012 and the 7th printing in June 2013, respectively.

On June 3, 2010, the defendant Qu Jianfang, in his capacity as "the copyright owner of the Avanti image" and "the legal representative of the former Avanti International Animation Company", issued a written explanation to the defendant Electronic Publishing House regarding the licensing of attribution matters under the aforementioned publishing contract. The main contents of this explanation were: 1. Avanti International Animation Company had ceased operations in accordance with national regulations, the company had been dissolved, and all remaining matters after the dissolution were handled by the legal representative, Qu Jianfang; 2. During the company's operations, regarding the business developed using Qu Jianfang's own copyright (including book publication, storybooks, comic books...), the company had signed buyout contracts for works made for hire with the writers, adapters, and illustrators and paid them remuneration. The above authors only had the right of attribution, and all other rights belonged to the company; 3. In the "Selected Stories", the cover, back cover, title pages, and full-page illustrations were all works by Qu Jianfang himself; 4. After the company's dissolution, all contracts for continued publication were signed exclusively by Qu Jianfang, and any copyright or attribution issues arising therefrom would be the responsibility of Qu Jianfang.

During the trial of this case, the defendant Qu Jianfang and the defendant Electronic Publishing House confirmed that, except for the right of attribution, all other copyright rights in the two books belonged to Qu Jianfang. Qu Jianfang stated that he would assume all rights and obligations related to the allegedly infringing books, and the plaintiff SAFS acknowledged this.

The Shanghai Xuhui District People's Court held at first instance that:

The character designs involved in this case, created by the author through hand-drawing, combine artistic elements such as lines, shapes, and colors to form specific and fixed character designs of Avanti, Bayi, and the Little Donkey, which meet the constituent elements of a work of fine art under China's Copyright Law. The character designs involved have distinctive features that differentiate them from other characters, can be separated from the films involved, and can be used independently. Therefore, the character designs involved are works of fine art that can be used independently. These works of fine art are still within the statutory protection period and should be protected under China's Copyright Law.

Based on the opinions and arguments of the parties, the issues in dispute in this case are: 1. Whether the three-dimensional puppet models in the films constitute a reproduction of the two-dimensional character designs; 2. The identification of the creator of the character designs involved; 3. The determination of the ownership of the copyright in the character designs involved; 4. Whether the acts of the two defendants in the main action, Qu Jianfang and the Electronic Publishing House, infringed upon the copyright of the plaintiff SAFS in the main action; if infringement is established, how should civil liability be borne; 5. Whether the plaintiff's lawsuit in the main action exceeded the statutory limitation period. Regarding the above issues, the court analyzed as follows:

1. Whether the three-dimensional puppet models in the films constitute a reproduction of the two-dimensional character designs

First, from the creative process of stop-motion animation films, both two-dimensional and three-dimensional character designs are based on the artistic foundation of fine art modeling. The character designs in the films involved initially appeared as two-dimensional character design drawings, which possess the basic elements of fine art works such as lines and colors, constituting independent works of fine art. Subsequently, three-dimensional puppets were made according to the finalized character design drawings. It can be seen that drawing the character design drawings is a key step in completing the three-dimensional puppets, and the three-dimensional puppet designs merely utilize the two-dimensional character designs. Given that only original external expressions can constitute works under the Copyright Law, although some technical processes and labor were involved in making the three-dimensional puppets, there are no differences or no significant differences between the three-dimensional puppet designs and the two-dimensional character designs, and thus they cannot constitute new works of fine art. Second, although the plaintiff SAFS argued that making the three-dimensional puppets involved various designs such as costumes, making them significantly different from the two-dimensional character designs, it failed to submit evidence proving the existence of objectively identifiable, non-trivial differences between the three-dimensional puppet designs and the two-dimensional character designs. In conclusion, the court determined that the three-dimensional puppet designs in the films are reproductions of the two-dimensional character designs.

2. The identification of the creator of the character designs involved

Although the defendant Qu Jianfang submitted evidence such as exploratory sketches and original manuscripts, these were not admitted due to deficiencies in formal requirements. However, proving the author of a work is not necessarily tied to the carrier of the work. In this case, first, the final script of the films involved and the opening credits of the films both identified Qu Jianfang as the art designer. The "Selected Works of Chinese Animation Character Designs" compiled by the plaintiff SAFS in October 1980 also credited Qu Jianfang as the author of the character designs involved. According to Article 11, paragraph 4 of China's Copyright Law, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, Qu Jianfang should be confirmed as the author of the character design works of fine art. Second, according to the evidence in the record, in July 1987, in a commemorative album for the 30th anniversary of SAFS's founding, it was noted that Qu Jianfang's design of the Avanti image was the most successful. In February 1988, in an evaluation opinion recommending Qu Jianfang for promotion to First-Class Art Designer, the first director of SAFS stated that Qu Jianfang was one of the most creative art designers, with representative works including Avanti. These facts indicate that Qu Jianfang created the Avanti artistic image. Additionally, the articles "A Preliminary Exploration of the Avanti Character Design" by Qu Jianfang, published in December 1980, and "Director's Notes on 'Avanti'" by Jin Xi and Liu Huiyi, published in March 1984, also reflected, to varying degrees, that Qu Jianfang independently created the works of fine art involved. Furthermore, SAFS admitted in this case that the character designs involved were drawn by Qu Jianfang, further confirming that Qu Jianfang created the character design works of fine art involved. Therefore, the creator of the character design works of fine art is Qu Jianfang.

The plaintiff SAFS argued that the character designs involved were created collectively by the director, screenwriter, and other personnel. The court held that while shaping a character design indeed requires unification with the character's personality as determined by the script and director and the film's style, design is the use of artistic techniques such as exaggeration, contrast, and decoration in the field of fine art to express the character's personality and identity through external expressions like lines, colors, and outlines, consistent with the film's style. In this case, the author used exaggerated and distorted artistic techniques to create character designs that express Avanti's wisdom, sharpness, eloquence, and witty humor, Bayi's greed, cunning, insidiousness, and stupidity, and the Little Donkey's lively and lovable personality traits, demonstrating the author's ingenuity and drafting skills, thus constituting works of fine art protected by copyright law. Therefore, the design of the character designs involved bore a strong personal imprint of the author, reflecting the author's individual thoughts, will, emotions, and artistic accomplishment. SAFS's argument that the character designs were collectively created by the director, screenwriter, and others lacks basis.

3. The determination of the ownership of the copyright in the character designs involved

The films involved were produced in 1978-1979, over thirty years ago. At that time, China was in a planned economy period, the Copyright Law had not been enacted, public awareness of copyright protection was generally weak, and the plaintiff SAFS had no regulations on the ownership of works. Against this backdrop, the determination of the ownership of the character design works of fine art created by the defendant Qu Jianfang must fully consider that there was no copyright law to rely on at the time of creation; the current legal concepts cannot be mechanically applied, as this would lead to deviations between legal facts and objective facts. In this case, the character design works were created by Qu Jianfang and reflected his personal will. SAFS produced no evidence to show that it made substantive changes to Qu Jianfang's character designs during the review process, so the works cannot be considered as embodying the collective will of SAFS. Moreover, the right of attribution for works created for a legal person belongs to the legal person, but SAFS repeatedly identified Qu Jianfang as the art designer or author of the works in the films involved, the final script, and the "Selected Works of Chinese Animation Character Designs". Therefore, the character design works involved cannot be deemed works created for a legal person. The determination of copyright ownership in the character design works involved should comprehensively consider factors such as the background and process of creation, the conduct of the parties and their true expressions of intent, and principles of fairness and good faith.

First, from the perspective of the background and process of creation.

On one hand, China had not yet established a copyright legal system at that time, and the public lacked legal awareness of copyright protection. As an employee of the plaintiff SAFS, the defendant Qu Jianfang created the works for the needs of SAFS's film production, and it was consistent with the general understanding at the time that the results of work created within the scope of duties belonged to the unit. The character designs involved needed to be designed according to the character's personality and film style determined by the script and director, and to some extent, they were the result of brainstorming by the creative team, incorporating the design ideas of the entire creative team. The intellectual contributions made by SAFS in this regard should be reflected in the copyright. On the other hand, as previously stated, the design of the character designs involved bore a strong personal imprint of the author, reflecting the author's individual thoughts, will, emotions, and artistic accomplishment. If the entire copyright in the character design works involved were attributed solely to SAFS, it would undoubtedly negate the original contributions made by Qu Jianfang in designing the character designs involved.

Second, from the perspective of the conduct of the parties and their true expressions of intent.

In March 2008, the plaintiff SAFS licensed others to use the animated images from "The Story of Avanti" on bank cards. It should be noted that although the character images in the films differ from the character design works involved, as their expressions vary with scenes, they always retain the most distinctive and identifiable features of the works involved, thus being substantially similar to the works involved without constituting new works of fine art. SAFS's licensing of others to use the animated images still constitutes use of the character design works involved. In July 2008, SAFS filed a lawsuit because others had published and sold "The Story of Avanti" VCDs with unauthorized use of the Avanti and donkey images on the packaging covers and disc surfaces. The above facts show that in 2008, SAFS authorized the use of the artistic images involved externally and enforced its rights against infringement of the copyright in the works involved.

Meanwhile, during the trial of Case No. (2008) Pu Min San (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 449 of the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court, the defendant Qu Jianfang, knowing that the plaintiff SAFS had licensed the Avanti artistic image to others for use on bank cards, explicitly stated that he would not assert his rights against SAFS. This fact indicates that Qu Jianfang was aware of and did not object to SAFS's exercise of copyright in the works involved prior to this lawsuit.

A large amount of evidence in the record shows that before the public release of the films involved, the defendant Qu Jianfang had used the artistic images involved to publish the comic strip "The Story of the Shadow" in the "New Youth" periodical and had drawn illustrations using the artistic images involved for the screenplay "Planting Gold—The Story of Avanti" published in the "Frontier" literary series. Subsequently, Qu Jianfang continuously submitted works using the artistic images involved for publication in publicly distributed works, used or authorized others to use the Avanti and other artistic images in the production of animated films, authorized others to use the Avanti and other artistic images on product packaging and in advertising promotions, or contributed them to mobile animation projects developed by others. On July 12, 1996, Qu Jianfang obtained a "Work Registration Certificate" for the Avanti artistic image. Regarding the plaintiff SAFS's assertion that Qu Jianfang did not use the artistic images involved between 1983 and 2003, according to the description of main achievements and major works (papers) in Qu Jianfang's "Senior Professional Technical Position Evaluation Application Form" for promotion to First-Class Art Designer in February 1988, a color single-volume comic book "Planting Gold" was published by Xinjiang People's Publishing House in 1983, and in 1986, he drew illustrations and layout designs for the book "Stories of Little Avanti" published by Shanghai Children's Publishing House. This content should have been reviewed by SAFS, indicating that Qu Jianfang used the artistic images involved during that period as well. In November 2004, December 2006, and October 2008, Qu Jianfang filed lawsuits against others for unauthorized use of the Avanti and other artistic images. Relevant websites and media widely reported on Qu Jianfang's participation in book signing events for the Avanti series books at the Shanghai Book Fair, interviews with Qu Jianfang, and final judgments by courts confirming Qu Jianfang's copyright in the Avanti artistic image, with media referring to Qu Jianfang as the "Father of Avanti" in their reports. Additionally, SAFS stated in this case that it had raised objections to Qu Jianfang's copyright registration with the Shanghai Copyright Bureau around 2008, but the bureau advised them to resolve the matter through litigation. At that time, considering Qu Jianfang was a long-serving employee, SAFS did not file a lawsuit.

Based on the above facts, the defendant Qu Jianfang continuously used or authorized others to use the artistic images involved over a long period, registered the copyright in the Avanti artistic image in 1996, repeatedly enforced his rights against infringement of the copyright in the works involved, and media widely reported on Qu Jianfang and the final court judgments. Given the extensive facts of Qu Jianfang's exercise of copyright in the works involved, the widespread media coverage, and SAFS's own statements in this case, SAFS could not have been unaware of Qu Jianfang's exercise of copyright in the works involved. However, SAFS did not raise objections or initiate relief procedures to assert its rights for a long time.

In summary, in the years prior to this lawsuit, both the plaintiff SAFS and the defendant Qu Jianfang engaged in acts of exercising copyright in the works involved, with each party knowing of the other's actions and not objecting. Over a long period, the two parties established a tacit understanding through their actual conduct that "both parties have the right to control the works involved," thereby forming a de facto contractual relationship. Based on the principle of good faith, neither party may subsequently make a contrary expression of intent, claiming that the copyright in the character design works involved belongs solely to one party.

In conclusion, considering the background and process of creation of the works involved, the parties' conduct in exercising copyright in the works involved and their true expressions of intent, as well as principles of fairness and good faith, the property rights in the copyright of the character design works involved should be jointly owned by the plaintiff SAFS and the defendant Qu Jianfang. Accordingly, SAFS's claim that the defendants Electronic Publishing House and Qu Jianfang infringed its copyright is unfounded. SAFS's claims based on its assertion of full copyright in the works involved are not supported by the court; Qu Jianfang's counterclaim seeking confirmation of his full copyright in the works involved is also not supported by the court. Pursuant to Article 4 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 3(4), Article 11, paragraphs 1, 2, and 4, Article 15, Article 60, paragraph 1, and Article 61 of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 4(8) of the Regulations for the Implementation of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, the court rendered the following judgment on April 8, 2015:

1. Reject the claims of the plaintiff Shanghai Animation Film Studio;
2. Reject the counterclaims of the counterclaim plaintiff Qu Jianfang.

Both Shanghai Animation Film Studio and Qu Jianfang disagreed with the first-instance judgment and appealed to the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court.

SAFS's appeal request was: to request the revocation of item 1 of the original judgment, and to remand the case for retrial or to reverse the judgment and support SAFS's claims in the original trial. SAFS's main grounds for appeal were as follows:

1. The dispute between the parties concerns the copyright ownership of the images of the three characters—Avanti, Master Bayi, and the Little Donkey—in the "Avanti" stop-motion film. The original court replaced the concept of "character image" (角色形象) in dispute with the concept of "character design" (角色造型). However, from the perspective of their formation timeline, creating the character design is only one of many steps in shaping the character image, while the character image is only finalized upon completion of the film. From the perspective of their connotations, the two-dimensional design and three-dimensional model are only part of the character image; they cannot encompass the personality traits such as language, actions, and character embedded in the character image. Furthermore, from the perspective of their creators, the appellant Qu Jianfang only drew the two-dimensional designs of the characters involved, while the creators of the character images were the entire production team of SAFS. Therefore, character design is not equivalent to character image. Article 15, paragraph 2 of the Copyright Law explicitly provides that only scripts and musical works are works that can be used independently from a cinematographic work. Character images are an inseparable part of the film and do not possess the same independence as scripts and musical works; they are inseparable from the entire cinematographic work. Although character images can be used on merchandise or other publications, regardless of the form of use, such use is never detached from the film and necessarily includes elements such as the character's personality traits and plot points. Thus, character images are not works that can be used independently under Article 15 of the Copyright Law, and their rights should belong to the producer, i.e., SAFS.

2. According to the content of the "Director's Notes on 'Avanti'" and "A Preliminary Exploration of the Avanti Character Design", the character images involved were created collectively by the production team of the films involved under the leadership and organization of the appellant SAFS during the production of the films. The appellant Qu Jianfang, as the art designer, was a key member and the draftsman participating in the collective creation. His attribution as art designer based on work division does not imply that SAFS acknowledged that Qu Jianfang independently created the Avanti and other character images. Therefore, even if the original judgment's determination that the dispute concerns the ownership of character designs is accepted, the character designs involved also meet the requirements for works created for a legal person under Article 11 of the Copyright Law, and SAFS should own the rights. Furthermore, even if Qu Jianfang is confirmed as the author of the character designs involved, the works are merely "special service works", and the copyright, except for the right of attribution, should belong to SAFS.

3. The production of the films involved and the design of the character designs occurred in the 1970s, when China had not yet established a copyright legal system. Indeed, the appellant SAFS and the appellant Qu Jianfang did not make explicit agreements regarding the ownership of the works involved. However, for the overall creation of the films involved, it conformed to the general understanding at the time that the results of work completed to fulfill job duties belonged to the unit. At the same time, during the film production, SAFS required creators not to submit works for external publication. Qu Jianfang admitted in the original trial that he did not submit works for publication during the filming period. The submissions found by the original court actually only indicate that relevant publications were published during that period, but do not prove that Qu Jianfang submitted works during that period. Qu Jianfang complied with SAFS's rules through his actual conduct. Additionally, evidence provided by SAFS demonstrates that from the completion of the films until now, SAFS has continuously used the Avanti character images as the copyright owner and enforced its rights externally as the copyright owner. In Case No. (2008) Pu Min San (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 449 of the Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court, SAFS, as a third party, explicitly denied that Qu Jianfang owned the copyright in the Avanti image and provided evidence proving that SAFS was the copyright owner of the Avanti image. Qu Jianfang explicitly stated in that case that he would not assert his rights against SAFS, and the case concluded with Qu Jianfang withdrawing his lawsuit. Subsequently, Qu Jianfang did not file an infringement lawsuit against SAFS. The above facts indicate that Qu Jianfang acknowledged SAFS as the copyright owner of the Avanti image.

4. The ownership of copyright is determined at the moment the work is created. Therefore, when the court of first instance examined the parties' conduct to determine the ownership of the copyright in the character designs at issue, it should have examined the parties' conduct at the time of creation of the works at issue, rather than the parties' use of the results after the creation of the character images at issue. Furthermore, according to the provisions of the Contract Law of the PRC, contracts are concluded by the parties by means of offer and acceptance. In this case, based on the facts found by the court of first instance, the Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio and the Appellant Qu Jianfang only had conduct in separately using the character images at issue, and neither party made any expression of intent to the other party regarding the allocation of rights in the character images at issue. There is also no fact indicating that either party made an undertaking of "both parties have the right to control." Therefore, the determination by the court of first instance that the Shanghai Animation Film Studio and Qu Jianfang had reached a "de facto contractual relationship" regarding the rights in the character images at issue lacks factual basis. The fact that the Shanghai Animation Film Studio did not interfere with Qu Jianfang's conduct of submitting the character images at issue for external publication and publishing after the completion of the filming of the films at issue does not indicate that it waived its rights, but only that it refrained from exercising its rights. The fact that the Shanghai Animation Film Studio did not assert its rights in subsequent relevant infringement lawsuits can only be understood in the same way and cannot be regarded as a statement on the issue of ownership.

5. The filming of animated films requires substantial investment and is extremely costly. However, the main part of the profit is not obtained through screening; its value is often also reflected in the character images created in the films. In this case, the Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio spent many years and invested enormous human and material resources in filming the "Effendi" series of puppet animation films. The creation of the character images at issue gathered the labor of many staff members of the Shanghai Animation Film Studio. The reason why the images at issue became household animated characters deeply loved by the audience is that their fame was based on the Shanghai Animation Film Studio's years of investment and continuous filming of the excellent "Effendi" series of animated films, and the public, extensive, and continuous dissemination of the films at issue and the "Effendi" images involved through forms such as cinema projection, television broadcasting, and distribution of VCDs, producing a good public effect. Conversely, according to the evidence submitted by the Appellant Qu Jianfang, his so-called method of promoting the Effendi image was mainly publishing books, and the time of publication was after 2004, when the fame of the Effendi image had already been formed. Moreover, the influence of books cannot compare with that of films and television. Therefore, Qu Jianfang only utilized and consumed the Effendi image, rather than promoting it. The determination of the court of first instance that the Shanghai Animation Film Studio and Qu Jianfang should share the copyright property rights in the character images at issue violates the principle of fairness. Furthermore, for the book "Effendi Classic Comics" alone, some readers commented: "It is not as good as the story version of Effendi," "The content inside is not much, and it is not very pure." Objectively, the Effendi image in that book has already deviated from the witty and humorous image of Effendi shaped by the Shanghai Animation Film Studio. If Qu Jianfang is allowed to continue the infringing conduct, the character images at issue, being state-owned assets, will be severely devalued. Therefore, from the perspective of protecting and promoting the character images at issue, it should also be adjudicated that the character images at issue belong to the Shanghai Animation Film Studio.

Qu Jianfang's appellate request is: to request the revocation of subparagraph (2) of the judgment of the court of first instance, and to amend the judgment according to law to support the counterclaim raised by Qu Jianfang in the court of first instance.

In response to the appeal of the Shanghai Animation Film Studio, Qu Jianfang's main defenses and grounds of appeal are as follows:

1. The artistic works of the character images at issue, such as Effendi, reflect a highly personalized artistic creation process. The creative process reflects the personal will of the Appellant Qu Jianfang, and does not comply with the provisions of Article 11 of the Copyright Law regarding works created for and in the name of a legal entity. At the same time, Qu Jianfang's creation of the artistic works of the character images at issue neither primarily utilized the material and technical conditions of the unit and was created under the responsibility of the unit, nor does there exist any law, regulation, or contract stipulating that the copyright is owned by the unit. Therefore, according to the provisions of Article 16, paragraph 1, of the Copyright Law, the artistic works of the character images at issue constitute general works made for hire, and the copyright is owned by the creator Qu Jianfang. The Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio only has the right to use them preferentially within its business scope.

2. According to the provisions of Article 15 of the Copyright Law, cinematographic works and works that can be used independently from cinematographic works are mutually independent, different works as stipulated by the Copyright Law. The Copyright Law has separately stipulated the attribution of their copyright. The producer enjoys the overall copyright in the cinematographic work, but it shall not interfere with the author of other works that can be used independently in the cinematographic work from exercising their copyright in accordance with the law. Character images in cinematographic works are works that can be used independently and can be separated from the cinematographic work. Moreover, this principle of copyright exercise has also been confirmed by effective judgments of relevant courts. The Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio's claim that it also enjoys the copyright in the artistic works of the character images at issue, on the grounds that it owns the copyright in the cinematographic works at issue, cannot be established.

3. Copyright is a legal right created by the Copyright Law, which came into effect in June 1991. The Copyright Law stipulates that if the rights of the copyright owner have not exceeded the protection period stipulated by the Law before the date of its implementation, such rights shall be protected in accordance with the Law. The character designs at issue were created in 1978, but the copyright in the works could only be created in June 1991 pursuant to the provisions of the Copyright Law. The attribution of the works should also be confirmed in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Copyright Law. The court of first instance confused the time of completion of the creation of the artistic works at issue with the time of creation of the copyright. It only considered the historical background of 1978 and did not apply the provisions of the Copyright Law to confirm the attribution of copyright in the works at issue, which is clearly erroneous.

4. Before the promulgation of the Copyright Law, the natural rights of the artistic works of the character images at issue, such as Effendi, including the right of publication, the right of authorship, the right of alteration, the right of reproduction, the right of adaptation, and the right of cinematography, were in fact all exercised by Qu Jianfang, and he received remuneration in accordance with relevant regulations. However, the Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio only used the character images at issue in the film field and never separately asserted or exercised any natural rights in the character images such as Effendi. When the Copyright Law formally took effect in June 1991, the character images at issue constituted general works made for hire under Article 16 of the Copyright Law. The Appellant Qu Jianfang registered the copyright in the Effendi character image, while the Shanghai Animation Film Studio did not undergo any copyright registration procedures for the character images at issue. Regarding the exercise of copyright in the character images at issue, Qu Jianfang and the Shanghai Animation Film Studio also exercised their respective rights in accordance with the provisions of Article 16 of the Copyright Law on general works made for hire. Qu Jianfang independently exercised the copyright in the character images at issue, and the Shanghai Animation Film Studio continued to exercise the overall copyright in the "Effendi" series of artistic films. In the case heard by the Pudong New Area Court in 2008, where Qu Jianfang sued others for infringement of his copyright in the Effendi character image, the Shanghai Animation Film Studio participated in the lawsuit as a third party. Later, due to the settlement among the parties, Qu Jianfang considered the fact that the defendant in that case was not the proper party and the litigation costs, and only then did he voluntarily apply to the court to dismiss the case. The fact that Qu Jianfang did not assert rights against the Shanghai Animation Film Studio in that case was based on his consideration that he had worked at the Shanghai Animation Film Studio for over thirty years. From this, it cannot be concluded that Qu Jianfang and the Shanghai Animation Film Studio reached a de facto contractual relationship where both parties had the right to control the copyright in the artistic works of the character images at issue. After the judgment in that case, Qu Jianfang continued to license others to use the character images at issue to shoot films and co-publish books. However, after experiencing the above litigation, knowing that Qu Jianfang had obtained the copyright registration certificate for the Effendi character image, had extensively used and authorized others to use the character images at issue, and that effective judgments of relevant courts had confirmed that the copyright in the character images at issue, such as Effendi, belonged to Qu Jianfang, the Shanghai Animation Film Studio still did not assert rights against Qu Jianfang. This indicates that the Shanghai Animation Film Studio recognized that the character images at issue were general works made for hire, and the copyright belonged to Qu Jianfang.

In response to the appeal of the Shanghai Animation Film Studio, the Appellee Electronic Publishing House argued: 1. Although the Copyright Law had not yet been promulgated and implemented when the artistic works of the character images at issue were created, according to the provisions of the Copyright Law, this case should still apply the Copyright Law. The character designs at issue can be used independently from the film. Existing evidence shows that the author of the character designs at issue is the Appellant Qu Jianfang. They are general works made for hire, and the copyright belongs to Qu Jianfang. There is no evidence indicating that Qu Jianfang and the Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio reached a mutual expression of intent to jointly share the copyright in the character designs at issue. 2. The Electronic Publishing House and Qu Jianfang agreed in the signed publishing contract on a warranty against copyright defects. Moreover, Qu Jianfang obtained the copyright registration certificate for the Effendi character image, and relevant effective judgments have also confirmed that Qu Jianfang is the copyright owner of the character images at issue. Therefore, the Electronic Publishing House has fulfilled its reasonable duty of care and should not bear tort liability.

The Electronic Publishing House expressed agreement with the grounds of appeal of the Appellant Qu Jianfang.

The Shanghai Intellectual Property Court, upon second instance, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Shanghai Intellectual Property Court held in the second instance:

The Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio claimed in the original trial that it sought protection for the copyright in the character images at issue, including both three-dimensional and two-dimensional forms. The Appellant Qu Jianfang clarified in the court of first instance that the object of his counterclaim in the original trial was the copyright in the two-dimensional images of the characters at issue, arguing that the three-dimensional images were reproductions and extensions of the two-dimensional images. Since the character images, whether displayed in two-dimensional or three-dimensional form, are all manifested as artistic works of character designs, the court of first instance defined the disputed ownership as the ownership of the copyright in the artistic works of the character designs at issue, which is consistent with the claims of the parties. The main issues in dispute in this second instance are: 1. Whether the character designs at issue constitute artistic works that can be used independently; 2. Whether the copyright in the character designs at issue should belong to the Shanghai Animation Film Studio or Qu Jianfang; 3. Whether the reasons for the Shanghai Animation Film Studio's claim that Qu Jianfang and the Appellee Electronic Publishing House committed infringing acts are established.

1. Whether the character designs at issue constitute artistic works that can be used independently

From the creative process of the films at issue, first, a two-dimensional design of the character image was formed, and then a three-dimensional puppet was made based on it for shooting, resulting in the final artistic film. The creator of the character designs at issue, for the first time, used hand-drawing methods, employing artistic elements such as lines and colors, combined with techniques such as exaggeration, resemblance, and deformation, to form specific, fixed character designs at issue. These designs have aesthetic significance, originality, and reproducibility, meeting the constitutive requirements for artistic works under the Copyright Law of the PRC, and should be protected by the Copyright Law. The court affirms the determination of the court of first instance, based on the evidence on file, that the three-dimensional puppet designs of the characters at issue constitute reproductions of the two-dimensional character designs. At the same time, although the character designs at issue can present different postures and changes in different scenes according to the script's arrangement, their basis remains the initially existing two-dimensional design. The subsequent numerous changes of the character designs in the film are merely uses of the pre-existing two-dimensional artistic work and do not alter the substantive characteristics of the two-dimensional artistic work, nor do they constitute new artistic works.

Article 15, paragraph 2, of the Copyright Law of the PRC stipulates that the authors of works that can be used independently from cinematographic works and works created by a process analogous to cinematography, such as scripts and music, have the right to independently exercise their copyright. Although this provision only lists scripts and music as examples, since the character designs at issue were formed before the film and, as artistic works, possess independent aesthetic value and can be extracted from the film for use, and in fact, from the multiple copyright infringement lawsuits filed separately by the Shanghai Animation Film Studio and Qu Jianfang as plaintiffs, it can also be confirmed that the character designs at issue were used by others independently from the film. Although after the character designs at issue were used in the film, a complete image with individual characteristics including identity, appearance, voice, and personality was formed, inevitably reflecting the personality traits endowed by the film, this only enriches the connotation of the character designs and cannot negate that the character designs, because they possess the constitutive elements of artistic works as stipulated by the Copyright Law, become works that can be used independently from the film.

2. Whether the copyright in the character designs at issue should belong to the Shanghai Animation Film Studio or Qu Jianfang

Whether it is the folk tales related to the characters at issue or the film scripts, both are literary works, and the descriptions of the characters at issue therein are textual descriptions. The Appellant Qu Jianfang, for the first time, portrayed the character designs at issue through hand-drawn expression, giving the characters at issue concrete form beyond abstract concepts or ideas, which possesses originality. Therefore, he should be recognized as the author of the artistic works of the character designs at issue. The analysis and determination of the court of first instance that the creator of the character designs at issue is Qu Jianfang and that the character designs at issue are not works created for and in the name of a legal entity are lawful and well-founded, and the court affirms them. The character designs at issue were created by Qu Jianfang, and evidence on file shows that he was an employee of the Appellant Shanghai Animation Film Studio at the time and created them to fulfill work tasks assigned by the unit. Therefore, the works at issue constitute works made for hire under Article 16 of the Copyright Law. The key issue in this case is the attribution of copyright in these works made for hire.

The character designs at issue were created before the implementation of the Copyright Law, when the copyright legal system had not yet been established. Therefore, in confirming the attribution of rights at the time of completion of the creation of the character designs at issue, it is not appropriate to directly apply the criteria for determining the attribution of rights in works made for hire set forth in the current Copyright Law. Otherwise, it may lead to a conclusion inconsistent with the actual expectations of the parties. At the time the character designs at issue were created, the public generally lacked awareness of copyright protection. As an employee of the Shanghai Animation Film Studio, Qu Jianfang created the works by completing work tasks in accordance with his duties, and in the absence of other agreements, the results belonged to the unit. This was consistent with the general understanding of the public at that time. However, the particularity of this case is that the Shanghai Animation Film Studio and Qu Jianfang asserted the attribution of copyright in the character design works through litigation over thirty years after the creation of the works at issue. Therefore, in determining the attribution of copyright in the works at issue, in addition to examining the social, legal, and institutional background at the time of creation, it is also necessary to deeply explore the parties' use, control, assertion of rights, and true expressions of intent regarding the character designs at issue during the entire period from the completion of creation to the filing of this lawsuit by the Shanghai Animation Film Studio, and to conduct a comprehensive review and judgment in conjunction with the principles of fairness and good faith.
